lessons.title: typedef
intro: typedef gives a type a second name: after typedef int Celsius; you can write Celsius t = 12;. Nothing new is created; Celsius is just int with a name that says what it means.
Its most common job is structs: typedef struct { … } City; lets you write City c instead of struct city c everywhere. Most C code since the 1980s does this.
You already used typedefs from the library: size_t (the type of sizeof) and FILE are both typedefs in the header files.

exercises.prompt: What does typedef int Score; do?
options: Makes Score another name for int
Creates a new kind of number
exercises.explanation: A typedef only adds a name. Score s = 10; is exactly int s = 10;.

exercises.prompt: Give the struct the name Point.
exercises.explanation: The new name comes after the closing brace, before the ;.

code: typedef struct { int w, h; } Box;

exercises.prompt: This program doesn't compile. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explanation: A typedef is a declaration, so it ends with a semicolon: } Point;

exercises.prompt: Why is typedef struct { … } Point; so popular?
options: You can write Point p; instead of struct point p;
exercises.explanation: It's only about reading and writing less, but in a big program that adds up.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a typedef from the C library?
exercises.explanation: stdlib.h says typedef unsigned long size_t; and stdio.h has one for FILE too.

lessons.title: enum
intro: An enum gives names to a list of related numbers: enum light { RED, YELLOW, GREEN }; RED is 0, YELLOW 1, GREEN 2. You can also choose values: enum { OK = 0, NO_FILE = 10, NO_MEMORY };, where NO_MEMORY becomes 11.
Compared with a list of #defines, the compiler does the counting, and the names belong together. Together with switch, it reads like a description of the program.
An enum is really just an int: printf("%d", RED) prints 0, and C won't stop you from storing 42 in an enum variable. To print a name, keep an array of strings next to it.

exercises.prompt: enum color { RED, GREEN, BLUE }; What is BLUE?

exercises.explanation: Each name without a value is one more than the name before it: B is 6, D is 11.

exercises.prompt: Print game over when the game is over.
exercises.explanation: The names are constants, not strings: no quotes. (OVER is 2, so 3 would be wrong too.)

exercises.prompt: Why use an enum instead of #define RED 0, #define YELLOW 1 …?
options: The compiler does the numbering, and the names belong together
exercises.explanation: Add a new name in the middle, and all the numbers move along by themselves.

exercises.prompt: This program should print GREEN's name but crashes. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explanation: c is the number 1, not a string. Use an array: char *names[] = {"red", "green", "blue"}; printf("%s\n", names[c]);

exercises.prompt: What does an enum variable really hold?
exercises.explanation: That's why %d prints it and why it works in a switch.

lessons.title: union
intro: A union looks like a struct, but its members share the same memory. It holds only one of them at a time, and it's as big as its biggest member.
In 1978, memory was expensive. A compiler's symbol table could store either an int or a double in the same place, depending on the symbol.

To know which member is valid, programmers keep a tag next to the union: a struct with an enum (what kind is it?) and a union (the value). This "tagged union" is how many interpreters store values, including the one running your programs here.

exercises.prompt: union u { int i; double d; char c; }; How big is it here, where a double has 8 bytes?
options: 8, the size of the biggest member
exercises.explanation: All three start at the same place, so the union only needs room for the biggest.

exercises.prompt: What's the difference between a struct and a union?
options: A struct holds all its members at once; a union only one at a time
A struct can't be in a union
exercises.explanation: Writing one member of a union overwrites the others.

exercises.prompt: Print the text only if the value really is text.
exercises.explanation: The tag says which member of the union is valid right now.

exercises.prompt: Why keep an enum tag next to the union?
options: To remember which member is valid right now
exercises.explanation: The union itself doesn't know what was stored last.

code: union u { int i; char c; };
exercises.explanation: i and c share the same memory. On today's computers, the lowest byte of 65 comes first, so c is 65 too: the letter A.

exercises.prompt: This program prints a strange number instead of hi. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explanation: The tag says it's a number, but the union holds text. Set v.is_text = 1; whenever you store text.
